title: Rituals That Signal Heightened Performance Focus
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Opening with a rapid catalogue of pre-performance rituals — Mike Piazza hitting fastballs at midnight on New Year’s eve, a CEO lying on a simulated bed of nails before big decisions, Suzanne Farrell pinching herself before going on stage, Greg Norman turning his driver headcover, Serena Williams’s five-and-two ball bounces, Wade Boggs drawing the Hebrew symbol for life in the batter’s box — the piece treats these not as superstition but as engineered transition cues. The argument is that a repeated physical action, once habitual, sends an unambiguous message to the mind that the moment for concentration has arrived. The claimed effects are specific: calmer mind, heightened execution awareness, reduced anxiety and increased confidence under pressure, and the shedding of doubt and distraction. The stick-shift image carries the point — the mind learns to slip into a higher gear on cue — and the essay closes by inviting the reader to invent such a ritual deliberately rather than waiting for one to form.
points: The examples are drawn deliberately from across domains — baseball, ballet, golf, tennis, business — to argue the mechanism is general rather than an athletic quirk.
Rituals are recast as transition cues: their content is arbitrary, their function is to mark the boundary between ordinary attention and execution focus.
The stated benefits are anxiety reduction and confidence under pressure, which the author attributes to the ritual becoming habitual rather than to the action itself.
The closing prescription is unusual in being an invitation to manufacture a ritual on purpose, treating it as a designable tool rather than a personal idiosyncrasy.
quotes: When he played for the New York Mets, former All-Star catcher Mike Piazza would start his year at the stroke of midnight on New Year’s eve by hitting fastballs in a batting cage.
Tennis star Serena Williams bounces the ball exactly five times before her first serve and two times before her second serve.
Rituals that signal an increased focus on execution are common among some best performers and leaders. These calculated actions send a clear message to the mind.
Such transition cues also reduce anxiety and enhance confidence in high-pressure situations and moments.
The habit of signaling to the mind that this is the moment for hyper-focus allows performers to shed doubt and distraction.
Like engaging a stick shift, the mind learns to slip into the gear required for top performance.
In high-stakes moments, nothing matters more than maintaining a singular focus on execution.
